findings.quote: sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together
findings.note: class 5/house style: the article spells out every other quantity ('thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water', 'two hundred and fourteen floating aids', 'forty minutes'), then switches to figures for this one; a sub-editor would normalise. Editor's rewrite: 'as much as thirty-five metres from their charted places'.

class 3 idiom/collocation: in a coastal-buoy context the intended sense is the flood tide at springs, but bare 'the spring floods' reads as seasonal river flooding; an editor would query the ambiguity. Editor's rewrite: 'through the spring tides' or 'on the spring floods'.

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3 idiom/collocation: bat boxes are put up, fitted or hung, not 'opened' — and the passage's own vocabulary elsewhere is 'went up', 'fitted between September and February', 'hang the finest box', so the one-off verb reads as a slip. Editor's rewrite: 'had been put up in June or July'.

findings.quote: through the spring floods, the buoys laid longest sit as much as 35 metres from their charted places for hours together
findings.note: class 3 idiom/collocation: 'the spring floods' is not the English term for the tidal state a mooring-swing figure would be quoted against. In British marine prose a 'flood' is the incoming tide and the periodic maximum is 'springs', so the tidal phrasing is 'at springs' / 'through the spring tides'; 'spring floods' reads as the Nordic snowmelt sense (varflod) carried into English. Editor's rewrite: 'through the spring tides, the buoys laid longest sit as much as thirty-five metres from their charted places for hours together'

class 5 house style: every other quantity in the piece is spelled out ('thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water', 'two hundred and fourteen floating aids', 'forty minutes'), with numerals reserved for years and the buoy's number; this lone figure breaks the pattern. Editor's rewrite: 'as much as thirty-five metres'

findings.quote: most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July
findings.note: class 3 idiom/collocation: a bat box is put up, fitted, hung or erected - it is never 'opened'. The piece uses the right verbs everywhere else ('they went up', 'those fitted between September and February', 'You can hang the finest box in the county'), so the odd verb reads as a slip rather than variation. Editor's rewrite: 'most of the boxes that failed had been put up in June or July'
